summary: Describes the state of the Internet from an architectural viewpoint, concentrating on end-to-end connectivity and transparency, and what happens when things like firewalls and translators break them. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: The Internet works best when messages go straight through unchanged. This explains why and what gets in the way.

questions: what is the end to end principle
how does nat break end to end connectivity
subtitle: How firewalls, NATs and other middle boxes eroded the Internet's end-to-end design, and the futures that might follow.

tldr.problem: The Internet was designed so packets travel from source to destination essentially unaltered, using one universal addressing scheme, but that transparency was being lost.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reviews the end-to-end argument, then lists the causes of lost transparency (Intranets, dynamic addresses, firewalls, private addresses, NATs, proxies, split DNS and load-sharing tricks) and the effects on applications and security.
tldr.outcome: It sets out three IPv6 scenarios (full migration, complete failure, partial deployment) without making recommendations, and concludes that partial IPv6 deployment avoids the dead ends of the non-IPv6 paths.

facts.label: Origin
facts.value: Input to the IAB network layer workshop, July 1999

today: RFC 2775 is an Informational memo from February 2000 and, according to its metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a snapshot of the Internet's architecture at that time and makes no recommendations.

sections.title: What Transparency Means
sections.content:
The memo analyses the Internet's "growing pains", often called "the end-to-end problem", by reviewing the network layer's progressive loss of transparency. Here, transparency means the original Internet concept of a single universal logical addressing scheme, and packets flowing from source to destination essentially unaltered.

Some causes are artefacts of the limited IPv4 address space, such as network address translation. Others, such as Intranets, are not. The memo was used as input to the IAB workshop on the future of the network layer in July 1999, so it does not claim to be complete and it refrains from making recommendations. It does not discuss routing implications, quality of service router state, or namespace issues.
sections.eli5: Transparency means a letter arrives exactly as you sent it, addressed the same way at both ends.

sections.title: Three Aspects of End-to-End
sections.content:
The end-to-end argument. Quoting RFC 1958, certain functions can only be performed correctly by the end systems themselves, so a network should accept some transmission failures and leave integrity to the endpoints. A design should not depend on state held inside the network; state should live in the endpoints and be lost only if the endpoint breaks (fate-sharing). The network's job is to move datagrams efficiently and flexibly.

End-to-end performance. Years of work on TCP led to comparatively minor changes to the protocol itself, but new transport protocols and quality of service models raise new questions. The memo notes these are not discussed further.

Address transparency. The catenet concept assumed one logical address space for the whole network, so packets could flow essentially unaltered and addresses could serve as unique labels. Some changes in transit, such as fragmentation or decrementing a hop limit, do not seriously harm the principle. But any change that needs per-flow state at an intermediate point violates fate-sharing. Addresses had also been built into transport checksums, cryptographic signatures, Web documents and licence servers. RFC 2101 concluded that IPv4 addresses can no longer be assumed globally unique or invariant, so designs that assume this will fail unpredictably.
sections.eli5: The smart work should happen at the two ends, not in the middle. The middle should just carry the mail and not need to remember anything about your conversation.

sections.title: Causes of Lost Transparency
sections.content:
The memo lists the developments that broke end-to-end transparency.

  • Intranets: private corporate networks, tightly controlled at the boundary. Many managers feel they alone decide which applications cross it, so address transparency seems unimportant.
  • Dynamic addresses from SLIP, PPP and DHCP: addresses are transient and must be forgotten after the session.
  • Firewalls: by their nature they fundamentally limit transparency. SOCKS (RFC 1928) lets applications cross one using a relay, so the remote server believes the firewall is the client.
  • Private addresses (RFC 1597, later RFC 1918): cannot be used across the public Internet without special measures. The memo calls the idea that they are a security feature a false argument, since a hidden address is just as private.
  • Network address translators (NATs): translation on the fly destroys end-to-end address transparency and breaks applications that carry IP addresses, such as H.323, unless an application level gateway is added.
  • Gateways, relays, proxies and caches: useful at the Intranet boundary and precise in how they interfere, but "involuntary" proxies that grab traffic without proper mechanisms are by definition not transparent.
  • Voluntary isolation, such as the WAP Forum, where devices connect through a proxy and never get end-to-end connectivity.
  • Split DNS: a name no longer maps to one address universally.
  • Load-sharing tricks: because IPv4 was not designed for anycast, tricks such as round-robin DNS are used and can interfere with name or address transparency.
sections.eli5: Many helpers stand between you and your friend: guards, translators, post office boxes. Each is useful, but each one changes or blocks something along the way.

sections.title: Effects on Applications and Security
sections.content:
The memo says it is impossible to measure how widely these mechanisms are deployed because many preserve the illusion of transparency, but they are in very widespread use. Firewalls, relays, proxies and caches have intrinsic value given the Intranet concept; the others are largely artefacts and pragmatic responses, costing the industry in administration and fault diagnosis.

The decline of transparency hurts end-to-end IP security. IPSEC cannot be deployed end-to-end in the general case: tunnel mode works between corporate gateways, and transport mode within a corporate network in some cases, but not across a NAT. NAT also breaks DNSSEC and Kerberos because they rely on address values.

Other effects: servers have fixed addresses while clients have dynamic ones, which favours client/server over peer-to-peer designs and leaves no easy solution for mobile servers. Mediating hosts such as a NAT or firewall violate fate-sharing and become single points of failure that need configuration data. Reverse DNS based anti-spam and priority policies keyed on addresses can be confused by translated addresses. All this adds complexity in applications, configuration, security and management, and makes faults harder to diagnose.
sections.eli5: When the middle keeps changing your letters, secret codes stop working, and when something breaks it is much harder to find out where.

sections.title: Future Directions and Conclusion
sections.content:
The memo sketches three scenarios.

  • Successful migration to IPv6: with an address space big enough for all needs, address transparency can be restored and transport-mode IPSEC can in principle deploy, though the Intranet/firewall model will persist. This is a very long term scenario, and it requires a viable partial-deployment scenario first.
  • Complete failure of IPv6: transparency cannot be restored. The memo examines re-allocating IPv4 addresses (with NAT and NAPT, realm-specific IP addressing at the host, or a "map and encapsulate" model) and an exhaustion scenario it calls a nightmare, with the Internet permanently fragmented.
  • Partial deployment of IPv6: IPv6 deploys only in some segments, and transition techniques become permanent. Addresses are sometimes 32 bits and sometimes 128 bits, and IPSEC can only deploy partially.

The conclusion is that none is clean or simple. The pure IPv6 path is the cleanest but hard to reach, the non-IPv6 paths all seem to end in dead ends, and partial IPv6 deployment, a required step toward full deployment, is messy but avoids those dead ends. On security, the memo says loss of transparency is both a bug and a feature: it blocks end-to-end IPSEC, but the Intranet boundary gives a well defined place to apply restrictions, at the risk of "crunchy outside, soft inside". Security above the transport level, such as SSL, SSH, PGP or S/MIME, is not affected by network layer transparency issues.
sections.eli5: There are a few ways the future could go. The memo thinks switching to the new, bigger addresses, even if only slowly and partly, is the road that does not hit a wall.

items.title: Successful IPv6 migration
items.text: Address transparency can be restored; firewalls and proxies stay.

items.title: Complete IPv6 failure
items.text: No transparency; NATs and patchwork, ending in possible fragmentation.

items.title: Partial IPv6 deployment
items.text: Messy mix of 32-bit and 128-bit addresses, but avoids the dead ends.
